### Describe the bug

`timeout` parameter exposed in `testclient.request` has no effect. Looking through the code, it seems as though we use the same interface as `requests` package but only a subset of those features are supported by `testclient`

```python
import time

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

mock_service = Starlette()


@mock_service.route("/slow_response")
def slow_response(request):
    time.sleep(0.01)
    return JSONResponse({"mock": "slow example"})


def test_timeout():
    """ no timeout exception raised -- this test passes when it should fail """
    client = TestClient(mock_service, raise_server_exceptions=True)
    response = client.get("/slow_response", timeout=0.001)
    assert response.json() == {"mock": "slow example"}
```

A TimeoutException should be raised if the timeout specified in request is shorter than the time the request takes.

### Actual behavior

No timeout exceptions are raised when setting timeout.

### Additional context

Eg. linked issues, or a description of what you were trying to achieve. -->

In CI/CD context, testing our own endpoints which, during integration testing, may timeout, is very helpful. If this is unsupported, it might be nice to have a list of differences between the interface of requests/testclient (this might include #1102).

I did look a bit how the requests package implemented their timeout exceptions, and to be completely honest I got a bit lost going down the rabbit hole of `requests` -> `urllib3` -> `http.client`.  Since we're using a different adapter for the testclient, it might be some work to reimplement all the way down the timeout exceptions in the same way.

Starlette is a web framework that supports both async and sync functions. The sync part code runs in a threadpool. The threadpool contains a maximum number of threads: 40. https://github.com/agronholm/anyio/blob/4f3a8056a8b14dbe43c95039a0d731ede1083cb7/src/anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py#L2071-L2077 The concern on this issue is that the threads are shared between the ones that handle the endpoint, and the background tasks. Assume we have a simple application: ```python from time import sleep from starlette.applications import Starlette from starlette.background import BackgroundTasks from starlette.requests import Request from starlette.responses import JSONResponse from starlette.routing import Route num = 0 def count_sleep(): global num num += 1 print(f"Running number {num}.") sleep(10) def endpoint(request: Request) -> JSONResponse: tasks = BackgroundTasks() tasks.add_task(count_sleep) return JSONResponse({"message": "Hello, world!"}, background=tasks) app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", endpoint)]) ``` Running it with `uvicorn`: ``` uvicorn main:app ``` And performing some requests (using [httpie](https://httpie.io/docs/cli)): ```bash for run in {1..100}; do http :8000 & done ``` We can observe that: 1. We can see `Running number 40.`. 2. Wait 10 seconds... 3. We can see `Running number 80.`. 4. Wait 10 seconds... 5. We can see `Running number 100.`. I'm just bringing this up, so people are aware. @agronholm proposed on Gitter that we create a separated `CapacityLimiter` dedicated only for handling the application (i.e. `request_response()`). This means that `n` (depending on the number of tokens we choose) number of threads would be dedicated for `request_response()`. > [!IMPORTANT] > - We're using [Polar.sh](https://polar.sh/encode) so you can upvote and help fund this issue. > - We receive the funding once the issue is completed & confirmed by you. > - Thank you in advance for helping prioritize & fund our backlog.

Originally posted by **aviramha** April 5, 2020 As discussed in the Gitter, my opinion is that starlette should provide a default limit for request size. The main reason is that without it, any Starlette application is vulnerable to very easy DoS. For example, newbie me can write a program as follows: ``` from starlette.requests import Request from starlette.responses import Response async def app(scope, receive, send): assert scope['type'] == 'http' request = Request(scope, receive) body = b'' json = await request.json() response = Response(body, media_type='text/plain') await response(scope, receive, send) ``` As a malicious user, I could send a 30GB sized JSON and cause the memory to go OOM. Other frameworks support this also - Django, Quart. My proposal is to add a default limit which can be overrided in the app configuration.

In our FastAPI tests we switch between different test users that we have as fixtures a lot, and I found that sub-classing TestClient is a nice way to switch between them via `client.as_user(user_42).get(...)` if I do this:

```python
class MyTestClient(TestClient):
    """Enhanced test client that can authenticate as different users via bearer tokens."""

    def as_user(self, user: User) -> Self:
        self.headers.update(create_access_token(user).headers)
        return self

@pytest.fixture
def client(db, test_user) -> Generator[MyTestClient]:
    app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = lambda: db
    with MyTestClient(app) as test_client:
        yield test_client.as_user(test_user)

    app.dependency_overrides.clear()

```
Unfortunately pyright gives this error incorrectly claiming that `client.as_user` doesn't exist:
```
 error: Cannot access attribute "as_user" for class "TestClient"
    Attribute "as_user" is unknown (reportAttributeAccessIssue)
```

The problem is that you have a hard-coded return type annotation on `TestClient.__enter__` that doesn't work with sub-classes:
https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/739ea4928b11d4b4cb2b366ccad11405ef3034c4/starlette/testclient.py#L670

I gather you can't use `typing.Self` yet?
Is there some other way to fix that type annotation?

For now I'll do a manual `typing.cast` as workaround.

### Bug

`FileResponse._parse_range_header` rejects a Range only when `start > end`, but `bytes=5-4` parses to the empty half-open range `(5, 5)` and slips past that guard. The result is a malformed `206 Partial Content` (`Content-Length: 0`, a backwards `Content-Range: bytes 5-4/...`) instead of a `400`.

`bytes=10-5` is caught (it parses to `(10, 6)`, so `10 > 6`), but the off-by-one boundary case where `end + 1 == start` is not.

### Reproduce

```python
from starlette.responses import FileResponse
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=5-4", 100)   # -> [(5, 5)]  (accepted; should be 400)
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=5-5", 100)   # -> [(5, 6)]  (valid one-byte range)
FileResponse._parse_range_header("bytes=10-5", 100)  # -> MalformedRangeHeader (already correct)
```

### Fix

The guard should be `start >= end` (an empty range is not satisfiable). A genuine one-byte request `bytes=5-5` parses to `(5, 6)` and is unaffected.

### Description

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B


c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)

# expected: a_or_b=B(x=1)
# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

If someone has an unsure instance of a namedtuple, they would need to re-validate it through type adapter, perhaps.
Or just use models directly on raw data -- for 99.999% of people this won't happen.

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py

class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.
